Why your senior dog hesitates at the stairs

Osteoarthritis is the most common cause of chronic pain in older dogs, and hesitation on stairs is frequently the first change an owner notices at home.

Owners often describe the dog pausing at the bottom of a staircase, taking the first step slowly, or refusing to go down while still willing to go up. Descending loads the forelimbs and the stifles differently from ascending, which is why the two directions can diverge.

Weight management, controlled low-impact exercise and environmental changes such as non-slip runners on hard floors are first-line measures. Analgesia is prescribed by a veterinarian after examination; dosing and drug choice depend on the individual animal and its bloodwork.

Hesitation that appears suddenly, is accompanied by yelping, or comes with hind-limb weakness is not assumed to be arthritis. Acute intervertebral disc disease and cruciate rupture both present this way and are time-sensitive.

A physical examination establishes which joints are painful and how the dog bears weight. Radiographs confirm degenerative change but do not by themselves establish how much pain the animal is in; owner-reported function over several days is a better guide to treatment response.
